questions.q: In the depolarizing channel with total error probability p, how is that probability distributed across the possible outcomes?
options: P(no error) = 1−p, and the remaining probability p is split evenly across X, Y, and Z, so P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=p/3
P(no error) = p, and X, Y, Z each occur with probability 1−p
Only X errors ever occur, with probability p, and Y and Z never occur
The probability is split evenly across four outcomes including two different identity operations
questions.explain: The depolarizing model assigns P(I)=1−p for no error, and splits the remaining probability p evenly across the three Pauli errors, giving P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=p/3 each.

questions.q: At a total depolarizing error rate of p = 0.01, what is P(X)?
options: Approximately 0.003333
Exactly 0.01
Approximately 0.99
Approximately 0.1
questions.explain: p/3 = 0.01/3 ≈ 0.003333 -- matching the lesson's worked table where p=0.01 gives P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)≈0.003333 each and P(I)=0.99.

questions.q: What does it mean for the depolarizing channel to be 'basis-independent'?
options: The channel's P(I)=1−p, P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=p/3 structure looks identical no matter which measurement basis (e.g., |0⟩/|1⟩ versus |+⟩/|−⟩) is used to describe the qubit
The channel never actually affects qubits regardless of what basis is chosen
The channel's error probability p changes unpredictably depending on which basis is used
The channel only applies to qubits measured in the computational basis and not in any other basis
questions.explain: Basis-independence means the same symmetric I/X/Y/Z structure holds in any basis -- this is exactly why the depolarizing model doesn't secretly favor one type of error over another, which is what makes it useful for fair threshold estimates.

questions.q: Why is the depolarizing channel the standard model used for threshold estimates in error-correction research, according to the lesson?
options: Because its basis-independence means it doesn't bake in an assumption that would make any one correction strategy look artificially better than it is, making it a fair worst-case stand-in for 'noise happens equally in every direction'
Because it is a precise physical description of real superconducting qubit noise with no simplifications
Because it eliminates the need for any error correction at all once applied
Because it only models bit-flip errors, which researchers consider the only error type worth analyzing
questions.explain: The lesson explains that the model's basis-independence makes threshold calculations fair and not accidentally tuned to flatter a particular code -- it's explicitly described as a simplification used for analysis, not a literal claim about real hardware.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how does real qubit noise typically differ from the symmetric depolarizing model?
options: Real noise is often biased, with dephasing (Z-like) errors occurring more frequently than relaxation-driven bit-flips (X-like), because T2 is often shorter than T1 in practice
Real noise is always perfectly symmetric across X, Y, and Z, exactly matching the depolarizing model
Real noise never includes any phase-flip (Z) component at all
Real noise is entirely deterministic and has no probabilistic component
questions.explain: The lesson notes that real hardware often shows biased noise -- Z-like dephasing errors tend to be more frequent than X-like relaxation errors because T2 is often shorter than T1 -- which is why some advanced codes are designed specifically around that asymmetry rather than assuming the symmetric depolarizing picture.
